paragraphs: At least one person was killed in an overnight attack on St Petersburg that hit two of the city's oil facilities, the BBC reports. Governor Alexander Beglov said fires were being put out at the St Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot, and that at least five people were injured. Russia's defence ministry said it shot down more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones over Russian territory overnight into Sunday. Kyiv had not yet commented on the strikes.

Other sites were also hit. A logistics centre belonging to the retailer Ozon and a regional data centre belonging to VK were targeted. Ozon said a drone caused a fire and staff were evacuated with no injuries. VK said its services were available as usual despite user reports of outages. Beglov said 12 apartment buildings and two homes were damaged, and Pulkovo Airport was temporarily closed.

The strikes follow a dispute over an energy ceasefire declared by President Trump last week. President Zelensky said Russia had targeted Ukraine's energy sector 76 times since the announcement. Ukraine paused its strikes on Russian oil facilities for three days, accusing Russia of continuing its attacks, then resumed them earlier this week. That drew Trump's anger, the BBC says, as he called for a truce to help a deal he struck with Vladimir Putin to supply diesel.

The US deal to import Russian diesel has strained Washington's ties with Kyiv. Zelensky suggested it amounted to the US investing in Russia's war effort, and some US Republicans have criticized Trump's temporary suspension of sanctions. On Sunday Zelensky said on Telegram that he had spoken with envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and that their teams were preparing the next diplomatic steps.

Both countries are hitting each other's energy infrastructure harder ahead of winter. Zelensky said Russia launched nearly 2,700 drones, 1,700 aerial bombs and 66 missiles in the past week, mostly at energy sites. Russia says it targets facilities used by Ukraine's military.

The French government held crisis talks on Sunday after one of the most violent days of unrest in years. Public buildings were burned, hundreds of shops were looted or destroyed, and police made arrests in cities across the country. The Guardian, citing the interior ministry, reported more than 2,000 arrests, while the BBC reported about 1,800. The interior ministry said more than 500 to 600 police, firefighters and paramedics were hurt. President Macron was due to address the nation Sunday evening.

Saturday's events had several strands. Large and mostly peaceful marches, which the BBC put at about 550,000 people, backed students' demands for more teachers and school repairs, and protested the cost of living. Separately, masked groups clashed with police, set fires and stormed buildings, and looters later ransacked shops. Town halls were attacked in Limoges and Marseille, and Lyon's tourist office was burned. Traders' groups said about 1,500 businesses were damaged.

Officials and opponents differ on responsibility. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez blamed several thousand far-left individuals and then delinquents who looted. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu and Marine Le Pen also blamed the ultra-left. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who joined the Paris march, said organizational failings by the government had opened the door to chaos. Lecornu called blaming police chiefs a dangerous and cynical reversal of responsibility.

Politicians on the left and right called for Nuñez to resign, according to the Guardian, and opposition figures questioned policing tactics and intelligence. Limoges mayor Guillaume Guérin said municipal police ran out of ammunition and called it a colossal failure of the state. A 17-year-old lost his right hand to a crowd-control grenade in Saint-Étienne. Macron's address is the next thing to watch.

Protests over living costs and housing that have shaken Spain and France in recent weeks spread to Italy and Portugal over the weekend, the Guardian reports. In Milan, a march against rising costs began peacefully but ended with masked rioters throwing stones and paving blocks at police and burning barricades. In Lisbon, hundreds of people set up a tent camp in Rossio Square.

In Milan, police used water cannon and teargas. LaPresse reported at least two officers injured and about 50 demonstrators detained, many of them minors. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said demonstrating was a right but setting cities ablaze was not, saying hooligans had exploited the protests. Milan's centre-left mayor Giuseppe Sala said the reasons for the protests were understandable but the violence against police and damage to the city were not justifiable.

In Lisbon, the camp followed a march that drew thousands nationwide and echoes one set up in Madrid three weeks ago. Protesters demanded action on housing, public services, pensions and wages. Official data show Portuguese housing prices rose 124 percent between 2015 and 2024, about twice the EU average. Prime Minister Luís Montenegro said his government understood people's outrage over what they saw as policy omissions, but warned against importing climates of instability that, he said, have no support in Portuguese society.

The Guardian also reports violent protests in Albania, where demonstrators angry over university conditions and tuition fees are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. In Spain, anger over rents grew after an 87-year-old woman was evicted. Rightwing parties then voted down the government's emergency housing measures, and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced a snap election for the end of November. In France, more than 1,200 people were arrested on Saturday, according to the report.

Former President Barack Obama accused the Trump administration of using the federal government against its political enemies in a post on X on Sunday defending Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn. His statement followed a federal search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home as part of a criminal investigation into her immigration status, Fox News reports.

Sources previously told Fox News Digital that investigators are examining whether Omar or her father committed fraud on immigration paperwork when she became a US citizen decades ago. Obama said she came to the United States with her father at age 12 and became a citizen automatically at 17 when her father was naturalized. He said investigators were pursuing an unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 at the time, which would have required her to apply separately.

Obama wrote that the government cannot selectively target people because of their political beliefs or what they say, and that the full weight of the federal government was being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she criticized the president. He pointed to federal actions involving New York's attorney general, a former FBI director and members of the Federal Reserve. He warned that if this became normal, future presidents of either party might do the same.

Fox News said it had asked the White House and the Department of Homeland Security for comment on Obama's allegations. Their response was not included in the report. President Trump has denied involvement, telling reporters the matter was up to the Justice Department. He also said, as quoted by Fox, that he had always found Omar to be totally crooked personally, but that this had nothing to do with him.

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee called a settler attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine a despicable act of terror and demanded arrests and prosecution, the Guardian reports. Levine, 63, was attacked last Friday by masked Israeli settlers using clubs and other weapons while she covered Palestinians harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank. She is recovering in a hospital near Tel Aviv from hand surgery and broken ribs. She said she was beaten for more than 10 minutes and that her camera, passport and phone were stolen.

A day later, settlers attacked European diplomats visiting the Christian town of Taybeh, according to the Guardian and the BBC. French mayor Bernard Baudoux was knocked to the ground. Belgium, France and Poland called on Israel to bring those responsible to justice. The EU condemned the attack and urged full accountability.

Israeli responses differed. The foreign ministry and the Israel Defense Forces condemned the violence against the diplomats, and the IDF said no soldiers were present. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar said the visit was not coordinated with the IDF in advance. Prime Minister Netanyahu's office urged caution about drawing conclusions and said it was concerned about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and Jewish residents of the West Bank. The Guardian says Netanyahu condemned violence against anyone but called the Levine attack alleged and its circumstances unclear.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot criticized Netanyahu over the violence ahead of the October 27 election. Police have promised an investigation. The Guardian cites the rights group Yesh Din saying about 94 percent of investigations into settler violence since 2005 ended without an indictment.

Prices of basic goods are rising quickly in Gaza as Israeli restrictions on commercial imports enter a fifth day, Al Jazeera reports. Israel said on Wednesday that commercial goods would no longer enter, amid a dispute over fees involving Palestinian merchants and Hamas, which still holds some authority in the territory. Families are stocking up on what they can find, fearing shortages.

Residents described sharp increases within days. Ismail al-Barawi, 52, said a carton of eggs rose from 35 shekels to between 60 and 70, and onions from five or six shekels a kilogram to between eight and 10. He said he now buys eggs in fours and fives instead of a full carton, and feared a 50 kg sack of flour could reach 200 to 300 shekels if the crossings stay shut. Iman Atallah, a displaced woman in Beit Lahiya, said a sack of flour had gone from between 25 and 35 shekels to about 80.

Gaza's Government Media Office rejected Israel's explanation. It denied imposing taxes or fees on commercial trucks and said the 10,000-shekel figure cited by Israel related to a voluntary community fund for vulnerable families. It said a 30 percent rate for cash transactions was agreed with the Chamber of Commerce to address a cash shortage and worn banknotes. It accused Israel of using the dispute to add restrictions and called on mediators to push for 600 trucks a day under existing agreements. Israel's side of the dispute was not set out in detail in the report.

The UN's humanitarian office, OCHA, reported that September food prices in Gaza averaged 204 percent above levels before October 2023. Residents said the new closure revives memories of the 2025 famine.

Violent protests shook Tirana for a sixth consecutive day on Sunday as Prime Minister Edi Rama, in his fourth term, ruled out resigning, Al Jazeera reports. Hundreds gathered outside the Ministry of Education chanting for him to resign. Police later used rubber bullets, water cannon and tear gas to hold back the crowds.

Protesters are demanding better education, more jobs, an end to alleged corruption and Rama's resignation. According to local media reports, demonstrators mainly attacked government institutions and police, including the Education Ministry building and the area around Rama's office. Shops in the centre have fitted metal shutters, and city workers removed paving stones to keep them from being used. The Ministry of Health said 65 people were injured on Sunday morning, 37 of them police officers, and that 272 people, including 169 officers, have been injured since Tuesday.

Rama said in a live social media stream that the government was not being challenged. He suggested the unrest could affect Albania's path to EU membership, which the country hopes to achieve by 2030, asking whether Albanians wanted this or the EU. He has blamed a foreign hand for the surge in protests and said his government is doing its best to address corruption. He said he was ready to listen to students' justified demands and discuss education costs, but that those who destroyed property must be held accountable.

TV Klan journalist Lindita Karadaku told Al Jazeera that both Rama and the young protesters were determined, and that no one could say what tomorrow would bring. The unrest follows months of discontent. The first protests this year, called the Flamingo Revolution, began in May against a luxury tourist complex project affiliated with Jared Kushner.

A fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday killed multiple people and injured others, according to Defence Minister David McGuinty. He described the situation as active and delicate and said high winds had worsened the blaze. He did not give casualty figures or a cause, and said he could not recall a similar incident in recent memory. The RCMP are involved in the investigation.

The military said casualty details would not be made public until its assessment is complete. Global News, citing unnamed military sources, reported at least seven dead and dozens injured after a gas line or gas well was hit during a live-fire training exercise. Officials have not confirmed that. A defence department spokeswoman told the BBC the situation continues to evolve and that there were no indications of terrorist activity.

The fire was reported at about 4 pm local time. The Municipal District of Wainwright said it crossed the base's fence and spread quickly in winds gusting up to 100 km/h. No evacuation order was in effect. Wainwright's hospital facilities were overwhelmed, and patients were taken to Edmonton, about 180 km away, where the Royal Alexandra Hospital declared a code orange. Dr Warren Thirsk called the situation a disaster. Air ambulances were sent from Saskatoon and Edmonton.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest training bases, with about 690 military personnel and 300 civilian workers on site on a typical day, according to CBC. Prime Minister Mark Carney said his thoughts were with those affected. Saskatchewan and British Columbia offered help. The armed forces said its immediate priority was notifying next of kin and supporting those affected.

Microsoft has withdrawn from a planned AI datacentre at Loughton in Essex, being developed by the British company Nscale, over concerns about power supplies, according to the Guardian. Microsoft had been expected to be the anchor tenant, and the Guardian reports that it told Nscale it was ending its agreement. The Telegraph first reported the end of the deal.

Ministers described the project as the country's largest AI datacentre when it was announced in 2025, and it was planned to open next year. A month ago it emerged that UK Power Networks had told Nscale it could not supply enough power to the site until the early to mid-2030s. The Guardian also reported in March that the location was still an operational scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the site.

Nscale said it remains "committed to both the Loughton project and the UK" and is exploring alternative power sources, including whether it can generate power onsite and speed up the connection process. A spokesperson said its relationship with Microsoft "remains strong and long-term" and that the grid issue has no impact on its other contracts. Microsoft is understood to remain involved in another Nscale project in Norway.

The Guardian says the loss leaves Nscale without its only publicly announced customer for the Essex site. It could also undermine the company's ambition to list on Wall Street this year at a potential valuation of $35bn. Nscale is backed by Nvidia, and Nick Clegg and Sheryl Sandberg sit on its board. The Guardian adds that a growing number of voices see such "neocloud" firms as a vulnerability in the wider AI economy. If the New York listing is delayed, it says, those concerns could come into sharper focus.

With just over two weeks until Election Day, Democrats have widened their once-narrow path to a Senate majority but still need to win several competitive races, according to Fox News. Republicans currently hold the chamber 53-47, so Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control.

Fox's Power Rankings show each party winning 47 seats, with six races rated toss-ups and three rated one step short of that. The toss-ups are Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio, Texas and Michigan. Republicans hold seats in six of the nine competitive races, so Fox says the GOP is playing more defense. Remy Numa, a Fox News contributor who steers the rankings, said that on polling alone any of the nine could be called a toss-up.

The three leaning races are New Hampshire and Minnesota, both Lean Democrat, and Kansas, Lean Republican. Minnesota moved toward the GOP this past week as Republican nominee Michele Tafoya appeared to gain traction. Numa said the map has expanded, mostly into red territory apart from Minnesota. Fox rates Georgia and North Carolina Likely Democrat, and says Republican outside groups have cut or pulled spending there.

Fox points to a difficult climate for Republicans, citing the tendency of the party in power to lose midterm seats, persistent inflation, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran, and President Trump's negative approval ratings.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee chair Kirsten Gillibrand said Democrats are in their strongest position yet. National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Tim Scott said the momentum is with Republicans. Fox says Republicans keep control by holding at least three toss-ups where they are defending seats.

U.S. defense firm Anduril could eventually manufacture its newly unveiled Steelfin interceptor missiles in Europe, a company executive said this week, according to Defense News. Brian Moran, Anduril's vice president for Europe, told Reuters on Monday he hoped Steelfin could become a capability the company engages on with Polish customers and industry, and that it would consider engaging European partners and customers.

Governments are trying to expand air defense production after conflicts exposed shortages of interceptor missiles. Wars in Ukraine and the Gulf have strained stocks and caused delivery delays. Anduril says Steelfin is due to undergo flight testing in 2027. Moran described it as a complementary system that could offer a more affordable interceptor alongside existing missile defense systems such as the Patriot.

Anduril is already in talks to set up production in Poland of its Barracuda-500 cruise missile, and Moran said that experience could open the door to further manufacturing projects. He described a very good experience with PGZ, Poland's state-owned arms group, and said discussions were also under way with the defense ministry and other government agencies. Poland, one of NATO's top defense spenders relative to the size of its economy, is seeking to expand domestic arms production and reduce reliance on foreign suppliers. Moran said the talks were focused on balancing local production with delivery speed and Poland's specific military requirements.

Asked about European calls for defense industrial sovereignty, Moran said the term can mean different things, from security of supply and maintenance to control over software upgrades and future modifications. He said sovereignty has a cost in money, timing and schedule, and that these must be weighed against the threats Europe faces. The military outcome matters most, he said.

Researchers say computer analysis shows "beyond any reasonable doubt" that William Shakespeare was the principal writer of Edward III, a play published anonymously in 1596, and that Christopher Marlowe also contributed, according to the Guardian. The study is by Rory Loughnane of the University of Kent and Brett Greatley-Hirsch of the University of Leeds.

It has long been thought that Shakespeare wrote at least a few scenes. The play was not in the 1623 first folio. Loughnane edited it for the 2016 New Oxford Shakespeare, which acknowledged that a couple of scenes were probably his. The new claim is that Marlowe is present too. Loughnane said this is the first time the case has been made seriously, and that it would change both the Shakespeare and Marlowe canons.

The team compared the play with securely attributed works by 10 dramatists active between the late 1580s and mid-1590s. In one test, 23 segments were identified as Shakespeare's and nine as Marlowe's. Rather than assigning particular lines, the study looked at linguistic features and the spread of marker words typical of Marlowe and atypical of other dramatists. The researchers say Shakespeare's segments may overlap with writing he did not do.

The analysis attributes a speech in scene 13, beginning "A sudden darkness hath defaced the sky", to Shakespeare, and a speech in the final scene to Marlowe. Greatley-Hirsch said the evidence is compelling because different forms of analysis repeatedly distinguish the two writers' language.

Loughnane noted that a 2016 study found Marlowe co-wrote the three Henry VI plays, and said the new finding suggests a more sustained working relationship than rivalry alone. The research will be published in Shakespeare Quarterly later this year. No independent reaction was included in the Guardian's report.

The Environmental Protection Agency has changed wording on its website that said the US had phased out two toxic Pfas compounds, Pfoa and Pfos, the Guardian reports. The page previously said the manufacture and import of Pfoa had been phased out. It now says quantities of Pfoa may be produced, imported and used by companies, and that Pfos remains in some limited, ongoing uses.

The change followed a complaint from the nonprofit Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, known as Peer, under the Information Quality Act. In a letter dated 18 September, EPA official Douglas Troutman wrote that the agency was updating its websites. The EPA did not immediately comment to the Guardian. Kyla Bennett, a former EPA scientist now with Peer, said the earlier wording was demonstrably false and welcomed the "candor" but called for enforcement.

The phase-out stemmed from a 2015 agreement between the EPA and eight producers, after litigation over DuPont's pollution in West Virginia. It was not a ban. Houston-based Inhance, which was not among the eight, makes up to 200m plastic containers a year. Peer testing and later EPA tests found Pfoa in them. The EPA ordered Inhance to stop production in 2022 and again by December 2023, but a federal appeals court overturned the later order, and Peer's lawsuit was dismissed because a judge ruled it lacked standing.

Inhance denies that Pfoa leaches at measurable levels and calls any Pfoa an "impurity". It says it cut such impurities by 90% and that third-party risk assessments found no unreasonable risk. Bennett argues the EPA should ban the chemicals, saying no safe exposure level exists in drinking water. The Guardian says the EPA appears to have stopped enforcement against Inhance.

A new generation of always-listening AI gadgets is raising legal questions about privacy and wiretap laws, CNBC reports. Devices include Amazon's Bee Frontier and Bee Eclipse, launched Thursday, Apple Watch Series 12 features such as Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Meta's camera-equipped glasses, and card-sized or pendant recorders from startups including Plaud, Pocket and Friend.

Makers say the products avoid earlier voice-assistant problems. Apple says its feature does not store audio, send recordings to its servers or involve human review. Amazon says it does not store audio from Bee devices. CNBC reports that some of these products can listen continuously and extract meaning from speech without keeping the underlying audio, which raises a largely untested question of whether that processing can itself be an unlawful interception.

Colin Zick, a privacy attorney at Foley Hoag, said many state wiretap laws turn on whether a communication was intercepted or its contents acquired, not whether a conventional recording exists. He pointed to Massachusetts, whose law covers devices that transmit, receive, amplify or record, and treats the substance and meaning of a communication as its contents. He said a device producing a written summary could potentially fall within that language. He noted that a bystander has not agreed to the maker's terms, and that in some states the greater legal risk may fall on the wearer.

Daniel Pi, a law professor at the University of New Hampshire's Franklin Pierce School of Law, said New Hampshire's statute covers the "aural or other acquisition" of contents, and he believes the Watch features would qualify. A user there could face civil or criminal liability, he said, though he stressed the practical risk is far lower and he would be surprised by prosecutions where no one was harmed.
Karen Panetta of Tufts University said that a wearer's own consent does not cover people around them.

Some conservative states, including Missouri and Iowa, have not taken up a hardship exemption to the new federal Medicaid work requirements, even though they have counties that would qualify, according to research from the nonprofit KFF cited by the Guardian. The Guardian said it had contacted both states' departments for comment; no response was included in its report.

The requirements take effect on 1 January. Adults covered through the Affordable Care Act Medicaid expansion will have to work, attend school, volunteer or do another qualifying activity for at least 80 hours a month. The law includes exemptions for people who are hospitalized, travel for medical care, or live in areas hit by disasters or high unemployment. New York City has adopted the high-unemployment exemption for the Bronx, where about 200,000 residents would otherwise have been covered by the requirements.

Experts offered several explanations. KFF's Jennifer Tolbert said officials who favor work requirements may think they should apply evenly to everyone, and that the exemption would require ongoing data reporting to federal officials and eligibility systems able to exempt people by county. Sarah Gordon of Boston University said the choice is partly political and reflects a patchwork, with some states trying to limit coverage losses and others not. Joel Ferber of Legal Services of Eastern Missouri said Missouri says it wants to avoid extra bureaucracy for participants, but he called that explanation illogical.

The Guardian notes that Arkansas introduced work requirements in 2018, and more than 18,000 people had lost coverage by the end of that year, while researchers found no significant rise in employment. Yale's Jacob Wallace said such rules generate paperwork that leads people to drop off the program.

Cities and states across the political spectrum are writing their own rules for autonomous vehicles as federal legislation remains stalled, The Verge reports in its Stepback newsletter. The result, it says, is a patchwork of regulations of the kind many industry leaders wanted to avoid.

The Verge notes that Nevada passed the first state law legalizing self-driving cars on public roads in June 2011, after lobbying by Google. Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards but have broad authority over street operations, and they are using it. Minneapolis is considering an ordinance requiring human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operation. San Diego's city council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and to give local agencies direct control of AVs in emergencies. Austin firefighters have raised concerns about the Tesla Cybercab's lack of a steering wheel or pedals and want rapid-response towing and direct communication with human operators.

The pushback is not limited to Democratic-led places. New York City, Chicago and Washington, DC have not legalized driverless cars, and The Verge says Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota and Iowa are among red states considering tighter rules. California lawmakers are weighing bills that would let cities limit fleet sizes or operating hours, and require emergency override access for police and fire departments. Culver City explored moratoriums on permits for AV fleet facilities, and Santa Monica used noise and traffic ordinances to restrict charging hubs.

Looking ahead, The Verge says developers are eyeing overseas markets, with Waymo planning London, Tokyo and Munich and Uber planning Manchester, Madrid and Dubai. Waymo, Zoox and Aurora are prioritizing states that bar city bans, and the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association is pushing for more preemption at the national level.
